additions.topics: Davidson-reference-2026; priority-high; research productivity; selection; diminishing returns; AER-forthcoming
additions.abstract: Models selection into research and studies how expansion in the number of researchers changes researcher composition. This provides an additional interpretation of declining measured research productivity.

additions.abstract: This paper presents direct measures of capital costs, equal to the product of the required rate of return on capital and the value of the capital stock. bresnahanbrynjolfssonhitt2002.use_in_axm: Supports a distinction between technology that helps workers and technology that replaces their tasks.
bresnahanbrynjolfssonhitt2002.limits_for_axm: Evidence on IT, organization, and skills is not an estimate of an aggregate AI--labor CES elasticity or of AI-industry revenue/GDP.
bresnahanbrynjolfssonhitt2002.notes: Targeted attribution check: pp. 339--342 and 370--371, September 16, 2026. See audit/ai_revenue_complementarity_2026-09-16.md.

brynjolfssonliraymond2025.abstract: Access to an AI assistant increases customer-support workers' productivity, with larger gains among less experienced and lower-skilled workers. Workers remain responsible for their conversations; the assistant provides recommendations rather than taking over the whole job.
brynjolfssonliraymond2025.topics: generative AI; worker augmentation; productivity; adoption
brynjolfssonliraymond2025.method: Analysis of the staggered deployment of an AI assistant to customer-support agents.
brynjolfssonliraymond2025.key_results: The published study reports a 15% average increase in issues resolved per hour; gains differ by worker experience and skill.
brynjolfssonliraymond2025.use_in_axm: Provides evidence that firms can adopt AI to assist workers, without inferring displacement from adoption alone.
brynjolfssonliraymond2025.limits_for_axm: It does not identify the aggregate AI--labor elasticity, aggregate employment and wage effects, or the AI-revenue/GDP ratio.
brynjolfssonliraymond2025.notes: Targeted attribution check: published pp. 889--893, September 16, 2026. The 15% figure is from the final published version, not the earlier working paper. See audit/ai_revenue_complementarity_2026-09-16.md.

ngaipissarides2007.abstract: A multisector growth model links uneven sectoral productivity growth to relative prices and structural change. When final goods are complements, relatively slower productivity growth can increase a sector's expenditure share.
ngaipissarides2007.topics: structural change; CES; complementarity; expenditure shares; relative prices
ngaipissarides2007.method: Multisector growth model with CES preferences and different sectoral productivity growth rates.
ngaipissarides2007.key_results: Equation (10) relates expenditure shares to relative prices and the elasticity of substitution across final goods.
ngaipissarides2007.use_in_axm: Illustrates why increasing quantities and falling prices need not increase expenditure shares under complementarity.
ngaipissarides2007.limits_for_axm: The elasticity is across final goods, not between AI and labor. The comparison is an analogy, not an empirical estimate or the same production model.
ngaipissarides2007.notes: Targeted attribution check: pp. 429--431, especially Equation (10), September 16, 2026. See audit/ai_revenue_complementarity_2026-09-16.md.

bea2018grossoutput.venue: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FAQ 1197
bea2018grossoutput.abstract: BEA distinguishes an industry's gross output from its value added. Subtracting intermediate inputs from gross output gives value added, which includes employee compensation and contributes to GDP.
bea2018grossoutput.topics: national accounts; gross output; value added; industry revenue; measurement
bea2018grossoutput.method: National-accounts definitions illustrated with an industry example.
bea2018grossoutput.key_results: Gross output includes intermediate inputs; value added excludes them. Employee compensation is part of value added.
bea2018grossoutput.use_in_axm: Distinguishes AI-industry revenue/GDP from AI value-added/GDP and the income accruing to AI owners.
bea2018grossoutput.limits_for_axm: This accounting definition does not measure AI-industry size or validate the model's calibration.
bea2018grossoutput.notes: Full FAQ checked September 16, 2026; published February 12, 2018. This is an official reference, not an academic paper.

acemoglurestrepo2018.title: The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment
acemoglurestrepo2018.topics: automation; tasks; labor share; wages; factor shares; endogenous growth
acemoglurestrepo2018.abstract: We examine the concerns that new technologies will render labor redundant in a framework in which tasks previously performed by labor can be automated and new versions of existing tasks, in which labor has a comparative advantage, can be created. In a static version where capital is fixed and technology is exogenous, automation reduces employment and the labor share, and may even reduce wages, while the creation of new tasks has the opposite effects. Our full model endogenizes capital accumulation and the direction of research toward automation and the creation of new tasks. If the long-run rental rate of capital relative to the wage is sufficiently low, the long-run equilibrium involves automation of all tasks. Otherwise, there exists a stable balanced growth path in which the two types of innovations go hand-in-hand.
acemoglurestrepo2018.notes: Excerpt from the official author abstract; the omitted closing sentences discuss stability and inequality with heterogeneous skills.
acemoglurestrepo2018.method: Task-based growth model with endogenous capital accumulation and directed innovation toward automation or new human tasks.
acemoglurestrepo2018.key_results: Automation displaces labor and lowers its income share; new human tasks generate a reinstatement force. Depending on relative factor costs, the long run can feature full automation or a stable balanced-growth path with both types of innovation.
acemoglurestrepo2018.use_in_axm: Canonical antecedent for the displacement--reinstatement mechanism and for the possibility that wages and labor's share move differently.
acemoglurestrepo2018.limits_for_axm: It does not separate inference from research compute, model monopoly rents, or characterize the delayed feedback-driven takeoff studied in the A×M paper.

jones2026future.abstract: Jones contrasts accelerated AI-driven growth with a continuation of historical growth and explains how complementary tasks can delay large aggregate gains even when automation feeds back into innovation. The essay discusses recursive self-improvement, distinguishes rising labor income from a vanishing labor income share, and considers redistribution and catastrophic risk.
jones2026future.metadata_source: Published JEP PDF supplied by the user; AEA article page
jones2026future.topics: recursive self-improvement; weak links; task complementarity; delayed takeoff; wages; labor share; redistribution; catastrophic risk
jones2026future.evidence_type: theoretical synthesis and illustrative task-based calculations
jones2026future.method: Economic-history comparison and a CES weak-link illustration drawing on Jones and Tonetti (2026), followed by discussion of labor markets, distribution and risk.
jones2026future.key_results: Remaining complementary tasks limit the output gains from automating other tasks. Early moderate growth can precede later acceleration as bottlenecks are automated. A vanishing labor share need not mean falling wages.
jones2026future.use_in_axm: Direct antecedent for delayed growth acceleration and for distinguishing wage levels from labor income shares. Helps situate the private RSI-investment mechanism and qualify novelty claims.
jones2026future.limits_for_axm: Its substitution elasticity is across tasks, not the aggregate labor--AI elasticity. It does not derive this paper's monopoly RSI equilibrium or AI-efficiency threshold, nor identify chi or validate its simulated dates. Catastrophic risk and heterogeneous ownership are outside this paper's model.
jones2026future.notes: Read all 20 PDF pages (printed pp. 3--22) on 2026-09-15; inspected the CES formula, Figure 2 and labor-share discussion visually. Main passages: RSI p. 5, weak links and delayed acceleration pp. 9--12, labor shares and distribution pp. 13--14. Published version, not the earlier NBER working paper. See audit/jones2026_connection.md.

chowhalperinmazlish2026.abstract: The paper studies how the prospect of transformative AI affects long-term real interest rates. Its consumption-based asset-pricing mechanism predicts that either rapid future growth or existential risk reduces the value of future consumption relative to current consumption and therefore raises long-term real rates.
chowhalperinmazlish2026.topics: transformative AI; real interest rates; consumption smoothing; asset pricing; existential risk
chowhalperinmazlish2026.method: Consumption-based asset-pricing model combined with cross-country evidence on long-term real rates and expected growth.
chowhalperinmazlish2026.key_results: Transformative AI is predicted to raise long-term real interest rates because either future abundance or existential risk lowers the marginal value of future consumption.
chowhalperinmazlish2026.use_in_axm: Provides a direct precedent for the positive relation between AI-driven growth and the equilibrium real interest rate.
chowhalperinmazlish2026.limits_for_axm: It studies expectations and long-maturity safe rates rather than the dated net marginal product of physical capital in the A×M equilibrium.

rachel2025.abstract: The paper develops a structural capital-market equilibrium model for the natural rate of interest in advanced economies. Its scenario analysis shows that an AI-driven productivity boom can shift capital demand and household saving enough to raise the safe natural rate by more than one percentage point.
rachel2025.topics: natural rate of interest; AI productivity; capital demand; saving; advanced economies
rachel2025.method: Capital-market equilibrium model with limited-foresight transitions and calibrated scenarios for productivity, demographics, fiscal policy, and risk premia.
rachel2025.key_results: The business-as-usual natural rate remains low, but the calibrated AI scenario raises the safe natural rate by more than one percentage point.
rachel2025.use_in_axm: Shows through a different macroeconomic mechanism that an AI productivity boom can raise the equilibrium real rate.
rachel2025.limits_for_axm: Its AI scenario is an imposed productivity process and combines several saving and investment channels absent from the A×M benchmark.

melinavilla2025.abstract: The paper estimates a DSGE model with ICT capital and uses alternative AI-investment scenarios to study output, inflation, and the natural rate. The natural rate rises most when ICT complements labor, by as much as 0.7 percentage points, while strong substitutability can make the response small or negative.
melinavilla2025.topics: AI investment; ICT capital; natural rate of interest; labor complementarity; monetary policy
melinavilla2025.evidence_type: estimated DSGE model and scenario analysis
melinavilla2025.method: Bayesian DSGE model that separates ICT from conventional capital and varies the elasticity between ICT capital and labor.
melinavilla2025.key_results: AI-related ICT investment can raise growth and the natural rate, but the interest-rate response depends on whether ICT complements or substitutes for labor.
melinavilla2025.use_in_axm: Supports both the positive interest-rate response and the claim that its sign depends on the labor--AI substitution margin.
melinavilla2025.limits_for_axm: ICT capital is a stock distinct from the A×M model's AI service flow, and the paper studies short-run natural-rate dynamics with nominal rigidities.

andrewsfarboodi2025.abstract: The paper studies U.S. bond yields around major frontier-model releases. Long-term Treasury and inflation-protected yields decline around releases interpreted as favorable news about AI progress, providing market evidence that complicates the standard prediction of higher real rates under transformative AI.
andrewsfarboodi2025.topics: transformative AI; bond yields; TIPS; event study; market expectations
andrewsfarboodi2025.method: Small-sample inference around major frontier AI model releases, separating releases interpreted as favorable news about AI progress.
andrewsfarboodi2025.key_results: Long-term nominal and inflation-protected Treasury yields fall around favorable AI releases and remain lower for several weeks.
andrewsfarboodi2025.use_in_axm: Provides a direct empirical counterpoint to the model's positive balanced-growth interest-rate response.
andrewsfarboodi2025.limits_for_axm: Event-study yield movements combine expectations, term premia, risk, and policy channels and do not identify the net marginal product of capital.

demireretal2025.abstract: Using API usage data from OpenRouter and Microsoft Azure, the paper documents rapid entry by models and providers, substantial price declines, persistent price dispersion within quality tiers, and frequent turnover among market leaders. It also finds horizontal and vertical differentiation across applications, preliminary short-run price elasticities slightly above one, and increasing experimentation with multiple models even though most firms concentrate usage in a single model.

korinekmckelvey2026.abstract: We construct a macroeconomic estimate of total AI production for the United States, combining inference and R&D/training activities and applying quality adjustments based on the evolution of API prices at fixed performance levels and the pace of algorithmic progress. We estimate that nominal AI compute spending grew over 140% per year each in 2024 and 2025, raw compute capacity grew over 200% per year, and quality-adjusted AI output grew over 2000% per year. These growth rates reflect expanding data-center capacity, continued improvements in chip efficiency, and rapid algorithmic progress.
korinekmckelvey2026.topics: AI measurement; inference; training; research and development; compute; algorithms; model capital; satellite accounts
korinekmckelvey2026.method: Macroeconomic measurement of inference and R&D/training, with quality adjustment for API prices, chip efficiency, and algorithmic progress.
korinekmckelvey2026.key_results: AI activity grows much faster after quality adjustment than nominal compute spending, because hardware capacity and algorithmic efficiency compound.
korinekmckelvey2026.use_in_axm: Provides the measurement vocabulary used to distinguish inference compute, research or training compute, algorithms, and model capital.
korinekmckelvey2026.limits_for_axm: It does not identify the model's substitution elasticities, derive equilibrium prices or rents, or validate the simulated transition timing.

acemoglurestrepo2019.topics: automation; new tasks; displacement; reinstatement; labor share; employment; wages
acemoglurestrepo2019.method: Task framework separating automation's displacement effect from the reinstatement effect of new human tasks, combined with an industry-level empirical decomposition.
acemoglurestrepo2019.key_results: Automation lowers labor demand and labor's share through displacement; new tasks raise both through reinstatement.
acemoglurestrepo2019.use_in_axm: Establishes the general distributional mechanism that the A×M paper takes as known rather than claiming as new.
acemoglurestrepo2019.limits_for_axm: It does not model AI-research feedback, rival inference and research compute, monopoly pricing, or delayed explosive growth.

karabarbounisneiman2014.topics: labor share; capital price; CES production; substitution elasticity; investment goods
karabarbounisneiman2014.method: CES capital--labor framework and cross-country evidence linking the relative price of investment to labor-share movements.
karabarbounisneiman2014.key_results: When capital and labor are gross substitutes, a lower relative price of investment can shift production toward capital and reduce labor's share.
karabarbounisneiman2014.use_in_axm: Provides the classic CES benchmark for why the location of an elasticity relative to one can change factor-share dynamics.
karabarbounisneiman2014.limits_for_axm: Its elasticity is between aggregate capital and labor, not between labor and quality-adjusted AI services; the two parameters are not empirically interchangeable.

aghionjonesjones2019.abstract: This paper examines the potential impact of artificial intelligence (A.I.) on economic growth. We model A.I. as the latest form of automation, a broader process dating back more than 200 years. Electricity, internal combustion engines, and semiconductors facilitated automation in the last century, but A.I. now seems poised to automate many tasks once thought to be out of reach, from driving cars to making medical recommendations and beyond. How will this affect economic growth and the division of income between labor and capital? What about the potential emergence of singularities and superintelligence? How will the linkages between A.I. and growth be mediated by firm-level considerations, including organization and market structure? The goal throughout is to refine a set of critical questions about A.I. and economic growth and to contribute to shaping an agenda for the field. One theme that emerges is based on Baumol's cost disease insight: growth may be constrained not by what we are good at but rather by what is essential and yet hard to improve.
aghionjonesjones2019.topics: artificial intelligence; automation; economic growth; bottlenecks; Baumol cost disease; singularity
aghionjonesjones2019.method: Task-automation extensions of growth models, including automation in goods and idea production and essential-task bottlenecks.
aghionjonesjones2019.key_results: Automation can raise growth sharply, but essential tasks that remain difficult to automate can bind aggregate growth for a prolonged period.
aghionjonesjones2019.use_in_axm: Early antecedent for the claim that bottlenecks can keep aggregate growth modest even while automation advances.
aghionjonesjones2019.limits_for_axm: The numerical automation path is exogenous, so it is not the closest precedent for the endogenous timing of the A×M takeoff.

trammellkorinek2023.abstract: Recent advances in AI may herald the near arrival of systems that can automate essentially all work. We review the macroeconomic implications of this scenario, in a framework synthesizing several strands of the relevant literature. Robustly, fully automating production alone (so that machines can self-replicate) would dramatically raise the growth rate and lower the labor share, breaking the Kaldor Facts that have long characterized frontier growth. Automating R&D (so that machines can self-improve) would accelerate the transformation, but may not produce it in isolation. Wages—the product of exploding output and a plummeting labor share—may rise or fall, depending on the returns to scale, the importance of natural resources, and the direction of technical change.
trammellkorinek2023.topics: transformative AI; production automation; research automation; growth; labor share; wages; natural resources
trammellkorinek2023.method: Macroeconomic framework separating automation of ordinary production from automation of research and development.
trammellkorinek2023.key_results: Full production automation can sharply raise growth and reduce labor's share; automating R&D accelerates the transformation, while wage effects depend on scale, resources, and technical change.
trammellkorinek2023.use_in_axm: Supports separating the production and research automation margins and distinguishing wage levels from labor's income share.
trammellkorinek2023.limits_for_axm: It does not use the A×M market structure or provide the paper's exact distributional decomposition.

davidsonetal2026.abstract: AI labs are increasingly using AI itself to accelerate AI research, creating a feedback loop that could lead to an intelligence explosion. We develop a general semi-endogenous growth model with an innovation network, where research and automation in one sector increase the productivity of research in other sectors, and derive a clean analytical condition under which growth becomes superexponential (``explosive''). We find that automating research can offset diminishing returns to ideas by activating two reinforcing channels: a technological feedback loop across research sectors, and an economic feedback loop in which higher output finances further research. Growth becomes explosive if the combined strength of technological and economic feedback loops overcomes diminishing returns. In a simple simulation calibrated to trends in AI progress, fully automating software research and modest (5%) automation in other sectors generates a singularity within six years. Bottlenecks do not overturn the result if task automation advances sufficiently fast.
davidsonetal2026.topics: AI research automation; innovation networks; feedback loops; spectral radius; explosive growth; compute
davidsonetal2026.method: Semi-endogenous innovation network represented by a nonnegative feedback matrix, with a spectral-radius classification of growth regimes.
davidsonetal2026.key_results: Technological and economic feedback can jointly overcome diminishing returns and generate superexponential growth; the criterion classifies the eventual regime rather than fixing a unique transition date.
davidsonetal2026.use_in_axm: Closest antecedent for the capability--compute feedback architecture, local feedback weights, scalar denominator, and explosive-growth threshold.
davidsonetal2026.limits_for_axm: Its automation shares and research allocations are exogenous in the economic application. Its network theorem is not the A×M equilibrium theorem, and its simulated dates are not transferable.

restrepo2025agi.abstract: This chapter explores the long-run implications of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) for economic growth and labor markets. AGI makes it feasible to perform all economically valuable work using compute. I distinguish between bottleneck and supplementary work—tasks that are essential versus non-essential for unhindered growth. As computational resources expand: (i) the economy automates all bottleneck work, (ii) some supplementary work may be left exclusively to humans, (iii) output becomes linear in compute and labor and its growth is driven by the expansion of compute, (iv) wages converge to the opportunity cost of computational resources required to reproduce human work, and (v) the share of labor income in GDP converges to zero.
restrepo2025agi.topics: AGI; compute; bottleneck work; labor share; wages; economic growth
restrepo2025agi.method: Long-run model in which AGI can reproduce all economically valuable bottleneck work using expanding compute.
restrepo2025agi.key_results: Once compute can perform all bottleneck work, growth becomes compute-driven, wages are tied to compute's opportunity cost, and labor's income share converges to zero.
restrepo2025agi.use_in_axm: Closest antecedent for the conditional limiting distribution in which the human bottleneck disappears and labor's share vanishes.
restrepo2025agi.limits_for_axm: It characterizes the endpoint, not the endogenous delayed takeoff, monopoly rents, or the split between inference and research compute.

erdiletal2025gate.abstract: Assessing the economic impacts of artificial intelligence requires integrating insights from both computer science and economics. We present the Growth and AI Transition Endogenous model (GATE), a dynamic integrated assessment model that simulates the economic effects of AI automation. GATE combines three key ingredients that have not been brought together in previous work: (1) a compute-based model of AI development, (2) an AI automation framework, and (3) a semi-endogenous growth model featuring endogenous investment and adjustment costs. The model allows users to simulate the economic effects of the transition to advanced AI across a range of potential scenarios. GATE captures the interactions between economic variables, including investment, automation, innovation, and growth, as well as AI-related inputs such as compute and algorithms. This paper explains the model's structure and functionality, emphasizing AI development for economists and economic modeling for the AI community. The model is implemented in an interactive sandbox, enabling users to explore the impact of AI under different parameter choices and policy interventions.
erdiletal2025gate.topics: AI automation; compute; endogenous growth; investment; integrated assessment
erdiletal2025gate.method: Integrated assessment model combining compute-based AI development, automation, semi-endogenous growth, investment, and adjustment costs.
erdiletal2025gate.key_results: The framework jointly simulates AI development, automation, investment, innovation, and aggregate growth across alternative scenarios.
erdiletal2025gate.use_in_axm: Main quantitative comparator for models that integrate compute, automation, investment, and growth.
erdiletal2025gate.limits_for_axm: It abstracts from the decentralized price system and market structure central to the A×M paper and does not supply its analytical regime classification.

jonestonetti2026.abstract: How much of past economic growth is due to automation, and what does this imply about the effects of A.I. in the coming decades? We perform growth accounting using a task-based model for key sectors in the U.S. economy. Historically, TFP growth is driven primarily by improvements in capital productivity. At the task level, capital productivity has grown approximately 4 percentage points per year faster than labor productivity in the U.S. private business sector, and substantially more in some industries. The main benefit of automation is therefore that we use rapidly-improving machines instead of slowly-improving humans on an increasing share of tasks. Looking to the future, we develop an endogenous growth model in which the production of both goods and ideas is endogenously automated and calibrate the model based on our historical accounting. Automation leads economic growth to accelerate, but the acceleration is remarkably slow because of the prominence of weak links, i.e., an elasticity of substitution among tasks substantially less than one. Even when most tasks are automated by rapidly-improving capital, output is constrained by the tasks performed by slowly-improving labor.
jonestonetti2026.topics: automation; weak links; task model; factor shares; endogenous growth; AI; delayed takeoff
jonestonetti2026.evidence_type: growth accounting, theory, and calibrated simulation
jonestonetti2026.method: Task-level growth accounting plus an endogenous-growth model in which production and idea creation are progressively automated.
jonestonetti2026.key_results: Weak links can make the acceleration remarkably slow even when most tasks are automated. Simulated aggregate paths can remain similar for decades before diverging; depending on the tail behavior and timing of automation, the capital share can converge to zero, one, or an interior value.
jonestonetti2026.use_in_axm: Closest dynamic precedent for the long apparent plateau followed by a steep takeoff and for the fact that automation alone does not determine limiting factor shares.
jonestonetti2026.limits_for_axm: Its elasticity aggregates tasks and its automation margin changes task assignment. That mechanism is not the A×M labor--AI CES, and its calendar dates cannot be imported.

kokotajlo2025.abstract: AI 2027 presents a scenario in which AI systems automate a growing share of AI research during 2027, rapidly produce systems with capabilities beyond those of human researchers, and create severe alignment and geopolitical risks. The scenario is a forecast exercise rather than an estimated economic model.

sevillaroldan2024.abstract: Epoch AI's expanded model database indicates that training compute for recent notable and frontier models grew by roughly four to five times per year between 2010 and May 2024. Similar growth appears across recent large language models and models produced by leading AI companies.

stanfordaiindex2025.abstract: The 2025 AI Index synthesizes evidence on technical performance, investment, adoption, responsible AI, public opinion, education, and policy. It documents rapid improvements in benchmark performance and falling inference costs while emphasizing persistent limitations in reliability, transparency, and standardized evaluation.

stanfordaiindex2026.abstract: The 2026 AI Index compiles evidence on frontier-model performance, compute capacity, costs, investment, industry structure, adoption, policy, and public attitudes. The report emphasizes the increasing scale of industry-led model development and the rapid growth of the physical and commercial infrastructure supporting AI.

iea2026.abstract: The report examines how artificial intelligence changes electricity demand, where data-center demand is concentrated, how AI may improve energy systems, and which infrastructure, efficiency, and policy choices determine its net energy effects.

nvidia2026.abstract: NVIDIA's Form 10-K reports the company's audited financial results, business segments, risk factors, and operating discussion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. For this project, the relevant evidence is the scale and growth of data-center revenue; the filing is not a measure of total AI-industry revenue.

iea2025.abstract: The report studies the electricity required by data centers and artificial intelligence, the geographic concentration of demand, the scope for efficiency improvements, and the ways in which AI could also transform energy production and consumption.

metrtimehorizon2026.abstract: METR estimates the length of software, machine-learning, and cybersecurity tasks that frontier AI agents can complete with 50 percent success, where task length is measured by human-expert completion time. The public release includes model-level confidence intervals and cautions that estimates above 16 hours are unreliable with the current task suite.

metrrebench2024.abstract: RE-Bench compares language-model agents with human experts on machine-learning research-engineering tasks under different time budgets. In the original evaluation, humans retained a large advantage at the longest budget even though AI agents were competitive at shorter horizons.

metrclaude2025.abstract: METR's preliminary evaluation tests Claude 3.7 on a five-task subset of RE-Bench. With a 32-hour budget per task, the agent matched the median score of human experts given eight hours, while METR emphasizes that the comparison is preliminary and not directly comparable with every earlier evaluation.

anthropiceconomicindex2025.abstract: The report analyzes sampled Claude.ai conversations and enterprise API usage to document differences in AI adoption across tasks, regions, and organizations. Its automation taxonomy distinguishes directive interactions from feedback loops and augmentation.

anthropiceconomicindex2026.abstract: The report introduces economic primitives for measuring AI use, including task complexity, human input, success, and interaction style. It compares multiple samples of Claude.ai conversations while warning that platform activity is not a representative sample of the economy.

cloudflareradar2025.abstract: Cloudflare's annual review summarizes changes in internet traffic, security, outages, and automated crawling during 2025. Its traffic measures count network requests and therefore should not be interpreted as measures of employment, task displacement, or economic value added.

holmstrom1979.abstract: The paper develops a principal-agent model in which effort is not directly observable and shows how informative performance signals shape optimal incentive contracts. It establishes the informativeness principle and clarifies why imperfect monitoring creates a tradeoff between insurance and incentives.
holmstrom1979.notes: No conventional abstract was available in the metadata consulted; this is an editorial synopsis.

solow1956.abstract: The paper develops a neoclassical growth model in which flexible factor substitution replaces the fixed-coefficient technology of Harrod and Domar. Its examples show how saving, population growth, and the shape of the production function determine whether capital intensity converges or continues to rise.
solow1956.notes: The publisher page provides an article outline rather than a conventional abstract; this is an editorial synopsis.

pitchford1960.abstract: The paper replaces Cobb-Douglas production in the Swan growth model with a constant-elasticity technology and characterizes how factor substitution changes capital accumulation, income growth, and the relation between growth and the saving rate.
pitchford1960.notes: No conventional abstract was available on the publisher page; this is an editorial synopsis.

jonesmanuelli1990.abstract: The paper develops a convex equilibrium-growth model with fixed factors in which the marginal product of capital need not converge to zero. It provides existence and characterization results and shows how tastes, technology, taxation, and trade can affect long-run growth.

rebelo1991.abstract: The paper describes endogenous-growth models in which policy differences can generate persistent cross-country differences in growth rates. Growth is possible without increasing returns because a core of accumulable capital goods can be produced without direct or indirect use of nonaccumulable factors.

duffypapageorgiou2000.abstract: Using a panel of 82 countries over 28 years, the paper estimates an aggregate CES production function and rejects Cobb-Douglas for the full sample. It finds greater capital-labor substitutability among richer countries and lower substitutability among poorer countries, while emphasizing that substitution above one does not by itself guarantee endogenous growth.

kruselletral2000.abstract: The paper estimates a macroeconomic production structure with capital-skill complementarity. Structures capital enters an outer production layer, while equipment capital is combined with skilled and unskilled labor in nested CES composites; changes in observed inputs account for much of the movement in the U.S. skill premium.
kruselletral2000.notes: This editorial synopsis emphasizes the production structure relevant for the capital-deepening benchmark.

raymookherjee2022.abstract: We study the long run implications of workplace automation induced by capital accumulation. We describe a minimal set of sufficient conditions for sustained growth, along with a declining labor share of income in the long run. The displacement of human labor is gradual, and absolute real wages could rise indefinitely. The results obtain in the absence of any technical progress and extend to endogenous technical progress.
raymookherjee2022.topics: automation; capital accumulation; labor share; wages; endogenous growth
raymookherjee2022.method: Long-run growth model with replicable physical capital, nonreplicable human capital, occupational mobility, and endogenous automation.
raymookherjee2022.key_results: Capital accumulation can progressively automate production, drive labor's income share to zero, and sustain indefinitely rising real wages.
raymookherjee2022.use_in_axm: Establishes that rising real wages can coexist with a vanishing labor share, a result the current paper does not claim as new.
raymookherjee2022.limits_for_axm: It does not model autonomous AI research, a monopolistic supplier of AI services, or the current paper's threshold between labor-bottleneck and AI-dominated equilibria.

gans2025aiknowledge.abstract: How does artificial intelligence affect the creation of new knowledge and long-run economic growth? This paper develops a general equilibrium model where AI enhances decision-making by interpolating between existing knowledge points. AI's impact on growth depends on a critical threshold in its capabilities: a modest interpolation range encourages incremental research and raises growth, whereas an extensive range promotes exploratory research that can reduce knowledge density and slow growth.
gans2025aiknowledge.topics: AI knowledge; research direction; capability threshold; market structure; economic growth
gans2025aiknowledge.method: General equilibrium model in which AI interpolates between knowledge points and changes incentives for incremental and exploratory research.
gans2025aiknowledge.key_results: AI capabilities generate a threshold between research regimes, and market structure changes the associated growth and welfare effects.
